card.hook: Here's the twist at Istiqlal Mosque: the best photo has a cathedral in it. Sukarno picked this spot so that Jakarta Cathedral and the mosque would sit across the road from each other.
card.stand_here: Stand on the front plaza of Jakarta Cathedral (Katedral Jakarta), on the side of the road facing the mosque, and face the mosque across the road. From Merdeka Square and the cathedral, the mosque is to the south-west, about 4 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the mosque, the road and the cathedral together. Then try 2x to pick out the white dome and facade. Use 0.5x only if you want the cathedral spires from up close, and check the edges, because shapes can look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white marble, then slide the brightness down a little so the facade keeps its detail instead of turning pure white.
card.best_time: Clear mornings or the softer light later in the afternoon suit white marble better than harsh midday sun. Early in the day there's usually less traffic and fewer people on the plaza too.
card.selfie_here: If you're allowed into the grounds, try the wide courtyard among the towering pillars with the mosque behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and check the backdrop when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the street side across the road from the mosque, where the cathedral is in the frame too, and pose with the buildings behind you; an underground tunnel links the two, so you don't have to cross the busy road.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed in most of the mosque, but it's restricted during Friday prayers and major celebrations. Avoid photos of people who are praying, skip the flash, and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the dome, the cathedral spires and the road all in one straight-lined shot without a single bus sneaking in. Take a few frames, because you'll need them!
card.good_to_know: Istiqlal Mosque is the national mosque of Indonesia and the largest in Southeast Asia, and it opened on 22 February 1978. Its name means 'Independence', and the central dome is 45 metres across, for 1945, the year of independence. A major renovation finished in 2020 cleaned the marble and stainless steel patterns, so it looks crisp in clear light.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the front plaza of Jakarta Cathedral (Katedral Jakarta), on the side of the road facing the mosque, and face the mosque across the road. From Merdeka Square and the cathedral, the mosque is to the south-west, about 4 minutes on foot.

card.hook: Picture a Ferris wheel turning over a patch of coast that used to be swamp and fish ponds. That's Ancol, and it's too big for one photo, so wander and snap as you go.
card.stand_here: Stand about 530 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From there you can take in the Ancol Dreamland skyline before you head in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for general scenes of rides and walkways, then try 0.5x for big structures or the open shoreline. Zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) picks out the Bianglala ferris wheel, signs and ride details from a distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put a ride or the ferris wheel on one of the thirds, then tap the brightest part of the sky and slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer light and cooler weather. The park lights can look good at dusk, and night mode helps if you stay on after dark.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera under or in front of the main entrance archway of Ancol Dreamland, and try 0.5x if your phone has it so you fit more of the arch in. The pier of Love Bridge (Jembatan Cinta) at Ancol Beach is another popular photo spot, especially at sunset over the water.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back in front of the main entrance archway while you pose under or in front of it, so the whole arch fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: Attractions such as Dunia Fantasi are ticketed, so check the official site for entry rules before you go.
card.challenge: Find a ride against a clear patch of sky and take the same shot at 0.5x, 1x and 2x. Then pick the winner and show it off.
card.good_to_know: Ancol opened in 1966 on land that was once swamp and fish ponds. It covers about 552 hectares and is described as the largest integrated tourism area in Southeast Asia. Dunia Fantasi (Dufan) opened on 29 August 1985 and faces the Java Sea.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 530 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From there you can take in the Ancol Dreamland skyline before you head in.

The Ancol photography note I found covers only flash use inside SeaWorld Ancol, so I left it out. The 'ask someone' spot is a sourced landmark, but no page gives the exact vantage point, so the position is a best reading. The second selfie spot is sourced for its sunset view, not for the landmark being behind the visitor. Lagoon Beach, the Dunia Fantasi zones and the Gondola were named as photo spots but without a usable framing, so I did not list them. The sources are mostly travel-aggregator and blog pages from different years, so check current access before going.

card.hook: Picture a slim white tower with a gold flame on top, and a huge open plaza that lets you step back and fit all of it in. That's Monas, and it looks best from a bit of a distance.
card.stand_here: Walk into Medan Merdeka (Merdeka Square) and stand in the north-eastern part of the open plaza, on the Istiqlal side. Face south-west, because that's where Monas is, rising from the middle of the plaza with the city behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the tower, the plaza and the sky in one go. Switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the tower with the city behind it, then try 2x to 5x to pick out the golden flame without walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the white marble doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or in the golden hour before sunset, when the sky has its best colours. The dancing fountain runs on weekend evenings, so that's a fun extra subject.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the stone blocks on the grassy area near the monument and let Monas rise behind you. Use the front camera, hold it low and a little back, and check the tower is behind your shoulder before you tap.
card.ask_someone: For a wider shot with the surrounding buildings in the frame, try the entrance on Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur near Gambir station, coming from the futsal courts side, and ask a passer-by to take it.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza is free to walk around, but the tower, museum and viewing deck may be ticketed or have restricted times, so check the official site before you go. Parts of the park may be fenced off for building work, so you may need to walk around them.
card.challenge: Put the tower on a gridline so it stands dead straight, and leave a little sky above the flame. Then zoom to 5x and take one shot of just the gold.
card.good_to_know: Monas is 132 metres tall and topped with a flame covered in gold leaf. It was built to commemorate the struggle for Indonesian independence, started in 1961 under President Sukarno, and opened to the public in 1975. The architect worked 17, 8 and 45 into its dimensions, for the proclamation date of 17 August 1945.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk into Medan Merdeka (Merdeka Square) and stand in the north-eastern part of the open plaza, on the Istiqlal side. Face south-west, because that's where Monas is, rising from the middle of the plaza with the city behind it.

card.hook: There's a real bronze elephant standing in the front garden of Jakarta's National Museum, and it's why everyone calls the place the Elephant Museum. Say hello to it before you do anything else.
card.stand_here: Stand in the front forecourt near the bronze elephant statue and face the pale colonial facade of the Gedung Gajah wing. If the elephant is in view, it should be right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the facade, and for the elephant too if it's in view. Switch to 0.5x if you want every column squeezed into the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the columns straight, then tap the white facade and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright and the walls look washed out.
card.best_time: Earlier or later in the day gives softer light on the facade and fewer people in the forecourt. Midday sun can be harsh on those white walls.
card.selfie_here: Head round the back to the sculpture garden (Taman Arca), where reviewers say the stone statues make the most photogenic backdrop. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let a statue peek over your shoulder. A TikTok visitor also loves the footbridge joining the old and new wings, but check that one when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Stand beside the bronze elephant with the Gedung Gajah facade behind it, and ask a passer-by to shoot from the forecourt facing you both.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in most galleries, but no flash. The treasury room (gold and ceramics) on the top floor is a no-photo zone.
card.challenge: Get the elephant low and off-centre with the white columns rising behind it, and no leaning walls. Bonus points if nobody's head sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1868, and the elephant was a gift to Batavia from King Chulalongkorn of Siam in 1871. Inside are about 141,000 objects, from prehistoric finds to Hindu-Buddhist statues. A fire in September 2023 closed it, and it reopened in October 2024, so the forecourt may look different from older photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the front forecourt near the bronze elephant statue and face the pale colonial facade of the Gedung Gajah wing. If the elephant is in view, it should be right in front of you.

card.hook: Two giant bronze figures are waving hello from the middle of one of Jakarta's busiest roundabouts, and you can't walk over to wave back. The trick is to go up and look down on them.
card.stand_here: Head for the Halte Bundaran HI Astra Transjakarta shelter and go up to the second-floor deck on its south side. The monument is about 165 m to the south, so face south and look down at the statues and the fountain ring.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the statues, the fountains and the roundabout in one shot. Then try zoom 2x for a tighter picture of the two figures and their raised arms. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want the whole circle and the towers around it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the figures on one of the vertical lines, and keep the horizon level, because the tall towers show every tilt.
card.best_time: Sunday mornings are Car-Free Day, when the roundabout fills with joggers, cyclists and street photographers. It's lively, but the deck gets busier and there can be queues. In the evening, switch on night mode.
card.selfie_here: The Bundaran HI Astra sky deck is a popular photo spot, with the statue, skyscrapers and fountain filling the background. Use your front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the monument over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of you with the statue framed by towers, ask a passer-by to shoot from the steps of the Grand Hyatt or Plaza Indonesia, but check the spot on a map first.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't walk up to the statue: it stands in a fountain surrounded by traffic, so shoot from the pedestrian bridge, the roadside plazas or the deck. You may need a Transjakarta or similar travel card to get through security to the deck, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Raise your own arms in welcome so they line up with the statues' arms, then see if a friend can catch you both in one frame.
card.good_to_know: The Selamat Datang (Welcome) Monument was finished in 1962 by the sculptor Edhi Sunarso, from a design by Henk Ngantung. It was built ahead of the Asian Games IV to show the country's openness to visitors. Each figure is about five metres tall, and with its pedestal the monument reaches roughly thirty metres.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Halte Bundaran HI Astra Transjakarta shelter and go up to the second-floor deck on its south side. The monument is about 165 m to the south, so face south and look down at the statues and the fountain ring.

card.hook: Most train stations look like they were painted by someone who hates joy, but Gambir went lime green on purpose, to match the park next door. It's a surprisingly photogenic building, and the colour does half the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand in the grounds around Monas on Medan Merdeka (Monas Park is about 410 m west of the station) and look south-east across the open square toward the station. Frame the green facade and the roofline from there.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the station and a bit of its surroundings. If the facade won't fit, tap 0.5x, and try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the green facade, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the green keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, before sunset, when golden-hour light falls on the green facade.
card.selfie_here: Look for the big 'GAMBIR' lettering on the station front and stand beside it, with the station and Monas in view behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the landmark over your shoulder. The exact spot of the sign is a best guess, so check it when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Monas grounds across from the station's Monas-facing side, so the whole station fits in the frame (it's about 410 m from the station, so expect a wide shot).
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your photos to the outside of the building. Gambir is a working station, so expect people and vehicles to pass through your frame.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, park the roofline on one horizontal line, and keep the phone dead level. Bonus points if nobody wanders through your shot!
card.good_to_know: The present station opened in June 1992 and replaced an older Art Deco one. Its modern design borrows from the traditional joglo style, with a lime green ceramic facade and moss green platform poles. The columns were placed so you can see the National Monument from Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur, and a station called Weltevreden opened on this site back in 1884.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the grounds around Monas on Medan Merdeka (Monas Park is about 410 m west of the station) and look south-east across the open square toward the station. Frame the green facade and the roofline from there.

card.hook: Most grand old buildings make you step back, then back again, then give up. This one sits behind a big open square, so the whole front fits in your frame with room to spare.
card.stand_here: Stand out on Taman Fatahillah, the old Batavia square, and face the museum's front. It fills the south side, so you can't miss it. If you can, line yourself up with the central fountain.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole front, the fountain and lots of open square in one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look. If people keep wandering into the picture, try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the domed cupola and the middle of the building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the building in the centre of the frame, so the symmetry looks deliberate and the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is best. Guides say the light is softer then, and the square is quieter. Weekends are busy, so a weekday gives you a cleaner view.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the open area in front of the museum's main front, or by the central fountain, with the building behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and step back so the cupola shows over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: You stand at the central fountain and ask a passer-by to shoot from elsewhere on the square, so the museum front fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't allowed inside the museum and indoor photography is restricted, so save your best shots for the square. Keep your valuables secure and watch for petty theft around the square.
card.challenge: Crouch down so the fountain sits at the bottom of your photo, then wait for a gap in the crowd and snap the museum with nobody crossing in front.
card.good_to_know: The building was finished in 1710 as the Stadhuis, the city hall of Dutch-ruled Batavia. It became a museum in 1974. It's modelled on the Paleis op de Dam in Amsterdam, which explains the dome and the formal, symmetrical front. Inside there are about 23,500 objects across 37 rooms.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand out on Taman Fatahillah, the old Batavia square, and face the museum's front. It fills the south side, so you can't miss it. If you can, line yourself up with the central fountain.

selfie_spots.why: Several guides single out the area in front of the museum as its iconic photo ground, and one blogger shows a visitor posing in front of the building for a portrait.

card.hook: Two pointed spires poke up above the trees in Central Jakarta, and the Istiqlal Mosque is right next door. It's a pretty unusual neighbourhood photo, and the cathedral is hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Walk onto the open lawn of Lapangan Banteng, the park the cathedral sits beside at its northern corner. Face north-west across the grass and the cathedral and its spires are right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both spires and the whole front in one shot. Switch to 1x if the building looks stretched. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the spire tops, the clock and the rose window.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they stand straight, then tap the plastered wall and nudge it a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the spires.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the west-facing front, which you can reach by walking round towards the Istiqlal side. Pick a time outside Mass, because photography isn't allowed during it.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Virgin Mary statue on the front side of the church and turn your front camera on yourself, so the cathedral sits right behind you. Try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the building over your shoulder. There are also fun pope and cardinal photo cutouts in the courtyard at the back, but check on the spot whether the cathedral fits in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the fountain pool in Lapangan Banteng and ask a passer-by to step back on the grass and shoot towards the cathedral, then wander a bit to find a clear gap between trees and lamp posts.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the outside from public areas are fine, but no photography during Mass and no flash. Keep a respectful distance from worshippers.
card.challenge: Get both spires standing perfectly straight on the gridlines, with a strip of lawn at the bottom, and then take the same shot from the other side of the building to see how different it looks.
card.good_to_know: The present church was built between 1891 and 1901, after the earlier building collapsed in 1890. Architect Marius Hulswit designed it in the neo-Gothic style, with cast-iron spires. The two tallest spires are 60 metres high, the middle one is 45 metres, and the south tower still has working old clocks.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk onto the open lawn of Lapangan Banteng, the park the cathedral sits beside at its northern corner. Face north-west across the grass and the cathedral and its spires are right in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a wide, car-free stretch of cobbles with a whole Dutch colonial city hall waiting at the far end. Fatahillah Square gives you room to step back, so the building actually fits in your shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the square and face south towards Museum Sejarah Jakarta, which sits on the south side. The old Batavia city hall facade will fill the view, with the middle of the square behind you to the north.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long facade and the open square in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look or when people are in the scene, then try 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) for windows, the roofline or the water pump.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the building's vertical edges straight, and tap the facade, then slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the building keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning, around 8-10 AM, gives soft light that shows off the building's details. Late afternoon works too. Midday shadows are harsh, and weekend middays are crowded, so expect people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Jakarta History Museum, use the front camera at 0.5x, and let the Dutch colonial facade fill the space over your shoulder. For a different look, try the colonial-style front of Cafe Batavia on the square in the hour before sunset, when the light is warm.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the central fountain in the middle of the square and ask a passer-by to frame you so the Jakarta History Museum fills the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are generally fine in the public square, but commercial or professional shoots might need permits. Flash is prohibited in the museum's period rooms. Some visitors warn about pickpockets in crowded areas, so keep your phone and bag close. Costumed performers expect a small tip if you photograph them.
card.challenge: Get two shots from one spot: first the museum with the cobbles leading your eye to it, then the water pump big in the foreground with the museum behind it.
card.good_to_know: The square was first recorded around 1627 as the Nieuwe Markt, or New Marketplace. The old city hall became a history museum in 1974, the same year the 18th-century water pump in the middle was restored. The name comes from Fatahillah, a 16th-century commander of the Sultanate of Demak.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the square and face south towards Museum Sejarah Jakarta, which sits on the south side. The old Batavia city hall facade will fill the view, with the middle of the square behind you to the north.

card.hook: Picture a stadium wearing a giant ring-shaped hat. Sukarno pushed for that roof so the crowd would stay in the shade, and it's still the star of the show.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in front of Gelora Bung Karno Stadium, facing its façade. Look for the archer statue in the foreground, with the stadium's roof and façade behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole roof ring in one frame. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner view with less edge stretching. For close-ups of the roof edge and the facade, try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep your phone level so the ring sits even instead of leaning, then tap the stadium and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives softer light on the roof. After dusk you may catch the facade lighting, so use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing. Midday sun is harsher and flattens the shape.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Bung Karno statue just inside the Gate 5 entrance, where fans often stop for selfies before going in. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in as much of the scene behind you as you can. A 2018 article also suggests a jumping pose with the archer statue, though it doesn't say exactly where that statue stands.
card.rules_and_safety: Access around and inside the stadium may vary, so check locally before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole roof ring perfectly level with the archer statue in front, then find the red, white and grey seats in a close-up.
card.good_to_know: GBK opened in 1962, just before that year's Asian Games, and is named after Sukarno, Indonesia's first president. It's described as the world's first football stadium with a circular roof. After the 2018 Asian Games renovation the seats are red, white and grey, like a waving Indonesian flag, and it now holds 77,193 people, down from 110,000 at opening.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, in front of Gelora Bung Karno Stadium, facing its façade. Look for the archer statue in the foreground, with the stadium's roof and façade behind it.

card.hook: Picture a row of bright white columns across a wide green lawn, with a flagpole and fountain dead centre. Merdeka Palace pretty much frames your photo for you.
card.stand_here: Stand in the southern part of Medan Merdeka, about 264 m to the east of the square's entrance point (about 4 minutes on foot). Face north across the lawn so the whole white front is ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade across the lawn. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the columns, the veranda and the flagpole. Save zoom 0.5x for when you're close, because the edges will stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white wall, then slide the brightness down a little so the palace doesn't turn into a flat white patch against the sky.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Guides disagree on which is better, so check the conditions on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the west side of the front of Istana Merdeka, beside the main lawn. Visitors posed there with the palace right behind them during the August 2025 Independence Day event. Use the front camera at 0.5x if you can, and keep the palace over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the foot of Monas in Merdeka Square facing north and ask a passer-by to take your photo. The palace is about 800 m away across the open field, so it will look small.
card.rules_and_safety: This is an active presidential palace, so plan to shoot from outside. The forecourt may not be open to casual visitors outside special events. Drones are not allowed. Expect barriers and crowds around 17 August.
card.challenge: Put the flagpole on the centre line, keep the columns dead straight, and see if you can get the shot without a single stranger in it.
card.good_to_know: The palace was built as the home of the Dutch governor-general, with work from 1873 to 1879. Jacobus Bartholomeus Drossaers designed it in a Neo-Palladian style. It took the name Merdeka in 1949, and it still hosts state events like the Independence Day ceremony on 17 August.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the southern part of Medan Merdeka, about 264 m to the east of the square's entrance point (about 4 minutes on foot). Face north across the lawn so the whole white front is ahead of you.

card.hook: Tall wooden hulls, a forest of rigging, cargo workers and stacked containers, all jammed into one frame. Welcome to Sunda Kelapa, where Jakarta's old sailing ships still do a day's work.
card.stand_here: Climb to the top floor of Menara Syahbandar (most often given as Jl. Pasar Ikan) and look out across the harbour. From the tower, the harbour is about 400 m to the north.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the whole harbour and the Kota Tua roofs. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view of the boats. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one pinisi hull and its rigging.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the line of moored boats along the lower third, with the Kota Tua roofs above.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely, when the sunset light settles over the harbour. It's also a good time to be up on the tower.
card.selfie_here: Head to the wooden jetty at Sunda Kelapa Harbor and stand with the traditional boats behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more of the boats in, and keep your shoulder out of the way. The small bridge that crosses to the ships also gives you a different angle.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed, but be respectful of the workers, keep clear of loading gear, and don't ask busy workers for portraits. Boats are loaded and unloaded during the day and heavy trucks drive along the harbour, so stay alert. The tower stairs are steep and visitors take turns, so be patient and don't linger at the top.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole harbour, then zoom in on a single boat for a second, simpler picture. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: Sunda Kelapa is the old port of Jakarta, on the Ciliwung River estuary. It was the main port of the Sunda Kingdom from the 13th to the 16th century, and the Dutch founded Batavia here in 1619. Today it handles only pinisi, the traditional two-masted wooden sailing ships that carry freight between islands.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Climb to the top floor of Menara Syahbandar (most often given as Jl. Pasar Ikan) and look out across the harbour. From the tower, the harbour is about 400 m to the north.

card.hook: The first thing to greet you at Taman Prasasti is a weeping stone woman, just inside the main gate. It's a quiet, slightly spooky welcome, and it makes a great first photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jalan Tanah Abang I, just inside the main entrance gate, and face the weeping female statue. The heart of the museum grounds is a little to the south-west of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the statue and the museum sign. Switch to 0.5x to fit the cannon and the building in together, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for carved details on the tombstones.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then make the picture a little darker if the sky behind it looks too bright.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows than midday. Check the opening times before you go, because the listings we found don't agree.
card.selfie_here: Head to the front of the museum building, by the old cannon and the museum sign, which is where visitors often take selfies. Use your front camera and hold it a bit low so the building shows over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a burial ground, so keep your voice low and never sit, stand or climb on the stones, because many are fragile memorials. Commercial or pre-wedding shoots need permits and may carry fees, so ask the museum office first. The ground is uneven, so wear comfortable shoes.
card.challenge: Find the tombstone with the most interesting carving or weathering, then fill your screen with just that texture.
card.good_to_know: Burials began here in 1795, and the cemetery officially opened on 28 September 1797. It became a museum on 9 July 1977. Olivia Mariamne Raffles, the first wife of Thomas Stamford Raffles, is among those buried here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jalan Tanah Abang I, just inside the main entrance gate, and face the weeping female statue. The heart of the museum grounds is a little to the south-west of you.

card.hook: Most Jakarta landmarks shout. Immanuel Church just sits there looking calm, with a big dark dome wearing a tiny white hat. It's up on a 3-metre foundation, so it looks like it's floating a little above the street.
card.stand_here: Face the church's front so the columns and dome line up in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole front with portico, columns and dome. If the pavement's too narrow to step back, try 0.5x, then use 2x or more (depends on your phone) to home in on the dome and white cupola.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the columns straight, then tap the columns and slide a little darker so the white details don't wash out against the sky.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is the recommended time for photos of the outside.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at the street corner on the pavement next to the church and tilt it so the dome and facade sit over your shoulder. You can also try the name board on the Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur frontage, where travellers often take photos, but the angle isn't confirmed, so check how it looks on your screen.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Gambir station forecourt, facing the church so the whole building is in view, while you pose on the pavement in front.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine, but be respectful of worshippers and services, and skip the flash. Drones typically aren't allowed near religious sites in cities without special permits.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole front, then one close-up of the columns, and see if you can make the church look even calmer than it already does.
card.good_to_know: Immanuel Church was once called Willemskerk, after King William I of the Netherlands. The first stone was laid on 24 August 1835 and it was finished four years later. It's built of brick in the Indies Empire style and counts among the oldest churches in Indonesia. It's a working church, so check the official site before you go to see whether it's open or being refurbished.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the street corner of Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur and Jalan Pejambon, near Merdeka Square, rather than shooting from the phone icon. Face the church's front so the columns and dome line up in one frame.

card.hook: Picture a bronze man with wild hair, mid-shout, snapping his chains with the whole sky behind him. That's the West Irian Liberation Monument, and it's hard to take a dull photo of it.
card.stand_here: Head into Lapangan Banteng in Sawah Besar and walk to the middle of the park, where the phone icon on the map marks the monument itself. The monument faces west, towards St. Ursula Catholic School across the road, so that's the side to look for.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole monument and its pedestal in one frame. Switch to 1x for group shots, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the bronze figure against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the pedestal up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then tap the figure and drag the brightness down a touch so the bronze keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or in late afternoon near sunset. Weekend evenings can get busy when the dancing fountain runs, so come early if you want clear frames.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the 'Jakarta Kota Kolaborasi' lettering, which sits directly in front of the monument, so the statue is right behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and tuck the figure over your shoulder. The amphitheater steps in Lapangan Banteng are another popular photo spot with the monument in the scene.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand on the open ground in front of the monument's base while you pose with the statue rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is open to the public, but the area around the monument's base has been closed off at times (the sides were closed in September 2023), so check current access before you go.
card.challenge: Crouch low, tilt your phone up and fill the whole sky with that shouting bronze figure, then copy his pose for a bonus shot.
card.good_to_know: President Sukarno commissioned the monument after the West New Guinea dispute, and it was officially unveiled on 17 August 1963. The design follows a sketch by the artist Henk Ngantung. The figure is about 11 metres tall and the whole monument is usually given as around 36 metres, but guides vary, so treat any height as approximate. The park was once a colonial parade ground, which is why there's so much space.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into Lapangan Banteng in Sawah Besar and walk to the middle of the park, where the phone icon on the map marks the monument itself. The monument faces west, towards St. Ursula Catholic School across the road, so that's the side to look for.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found gives a specific photographer position that frames the whole monument, so the passer-by spot is a general area, not a precise framing point; ask-someone spot is only loosely supported. The Kompas 2023 visit found the monument's left and right sides closed, so the approach may vary. Some pages are older (2018 renovation coverage; 2023 Kompas), so check current access. No selfie stick or tripod rules were stated on any page I found. Coordinates from Evendo (-6.1702984, 106.8349253) match the given position. Some sources conflict on the monument's height (36 m pedestal, about 50 m total per one blog; 9 m statue per Kompas). I did not verify which side of the monument the amphitheater sits on, so the selfie direction at the steps is unconfirmed.
